To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) information asymmetries are a significant barrier to applying for merit-based funding, (2) information on the details of the application procedure increases the application rate of non-academic and of male students, and (3) general information on the funding system increases the likelihood to apply for alternative sources of funding.

(i) information asymmetries about federally funded merit-based scholarship programs exist, (ii) these asymmetries are reduced by information on the application process, (iii) the information treatment increases application rates for the targeted scholarships, and (iv) the information treatment triggers participants' information search and increases application rates for alternative funding sources.
(1) information asymmetries do exist and (2) tailored information, conveyed by a role model, can increase students' application rates for merit-based scholarships.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of information in the application process for merit-based aid.
the potential of merit-based scholarships to foster social mobility and the role of information in the application process.
the role of information in the application process of merit-based scholarships.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
providing tailored information by role models increases the likelihood of non-academic and/or male students to apply for federally funded merit scholarships.
the role model treatment increased the number of applications for merit-based aid and the general information treatment did not, but increased the number of non-merit-based applications.
providing information on merit-based aid increases the number of applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

information asymmetries can be reduced and that information on the application procedure increases application rates for merit-based scholarships, particularly among non-academic and young male students.
information on the application process is key to increasing merit-based aid for non-academic and low-SES students.
providing information to students about merit-based aid is a promising policy tool for improving access to higher education for talented students of non- academic backgrounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
information asymmetries are a major impediment for students' participation in merit-based aid programs.
the application for merit-based aid is not only about money.
information asymmetries do exist and that they can be addressed by targeted interventions.
